California voters rejected Proposition 40, the billionaire tax, which had divided Democrats with opponents saying it would drive the wealthy from the state.
Jae C. Hong/AP

Jae C. Hong/AP
Midterms coverage: Live results | Stories around the country Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app
California voters have rejected a proposal to charge billionaires a one-time 5% tax on most of their wealth, according to a race call by The Associated Press.
Proponents said the tax could raise $100 billion for healthcare. Led by a union that represents healthcare workers, the SEIU-UHW, advocates of the tax said the Republican-controlled Congress cut healthcare programs to give tax breaks to the wealthy, so it was time for the wealthy in California to fill the gap. The state has more than 200 billionaires, according to estimates, with some putting the number at a few hundred.
Opponents argued that the proposal, known as Prop 40, would just drive the wealthy out of California, costing the state revenue and harming its economy.

France is accusing Iran of having launched a series of destructive cyberattacks against its critical infrastructure in October.
According to the French National Cybersecurity Agency, ANSSI, Iranian military hackers took over refrigeration controllers at around 700 different retail sites in France, from supermarkets to butcher shops, turning up the temperature in the middle of the night and spoiling millions of dollars' worth of food.
They also targeted several small hydroelectric power plants, resulting in "moderate effects," wrote ANSSI in its press release.

Supreme Court says border wall construction can continue in west Texas

In September, Texas landowners filed a separate lawsuit over the federal government's border barrier plans in the Big Bend area, claiming their constitutional rights are being violated.
Carlos Morales

The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday allowed the Trump administration to continue with its plans to construct hundreds of miles of border barrier and security infrastructure in west Texas, while a court hearing over the effort moves forward.
The federal government's plans have stirred bipartisan backlash for its inclusion of Big Bend National Park, a beloved stretch of public land known for its sweeping canyons and unspoiled desert landscape.
In a five-page decision issued Monday, the high court wrote that the federal judge who ruled on the order didn't have the authority to weigh in.
"The injunction thus impedes the Government from advancing its 'compelling interests' in border security and integrity," reads the unsigned decision. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the lone dissenter in the decision.

item.title: Thick smog shrouds New Delhi after Diwali firecrackers add to seasonal pollution
item.description:
Asia
Thick smog shrouds New Delhi after Diwali firecrackers add to seasonal pollution
November 9, 202610:09 AM ET
By
The Associated Press
People walk in front of India Gate, shrouded in thick smog after firecrackers lit up the sky overnight during Diwali celebrations, in New Delhi, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026.
Manish Swarup/AP
hide caption
toggle caption i
Manish Swarup/AP
NEW DELHI — A thick blanket of smog shrouded India's capital Monday after firecrackers lit up the skies over New Delhi during Diwali celebrations, compounding dangerously high pollution levels and intensifying the seasonal air pollution crisis that grips the city every year.
Despite restrictions on fireworks, residents in New Delhi celebrated the Hindu festival of lights with firecrackers on Sunday evening, releasing smoke and fine particulate matter into the atmosphere. The air quality index exceeded 350 in several parts of the capital on Monday morning, reaching the severe category and posing significant health risks.
Monitoring stations across the city recorded similarly alarming levels, while visibility deteriorated as a gray haze blanketed streets and high-rise buildings.

item.title: British comedian Russell Brand sentenced to over 10 years for rape and sexual assault
item.description:

British comedian Russell Brand sentenced to over 10 years for rape and sexual assault
November 9, 20269:36 AM ET
By
Kate Bartlett
This is a court artist sketch by Elizabeth Cook of Russell Brand in the dock at Southwark Crown Court, in London, on Nov. 5.
Elizabeth Cook/PA/AP
hide caption
toggle caption i
Elizabeth Cook/PA/AP
Russell Brand, the raunchy, irreverent British comedian who became a celebrity darling in the early 2000s, has been sentenced to over 10 years in prison after being found guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
"The total sentence is one of ten years, six months," said Judge Justice Bennathan on handing down the sentence at Southwark Crown Court in London on Monday.
Brand, 51, was a career chameleon who went from stand-up comic and MTV host to a political analyst esteemed by Britain's left, only to become a conspiracy theorist and Christian convert beloved by the U.S. right.
But critics of Brand said there was always a clear thread of misogyny running through his comedy routines, and that his mistreatment of women had been an open secret for decades.
Over the past four weeks, six women testified against the comedian in court in London, in a trial that garnered massive media attention.

item.title: On wild Cumberland Island, a land swap proposal stirs controversy
item.description:
American Identity
On wild Cumberland Island, a land swap proposal stirs controversy
November 9, 20265:00 AM ET
By
Debbie Elliott
,
Liz Baker
A wild horse grazes on whatever food it can find on Cumberland Island, Ga. on Oct 8, 2026. The National Park Service, which has managed the island since 1972, recently proposed a land swap with descendants of Thomas Carnegie, the wealthy Gilded Age industrialist who built homes on the island.
Malcolm Jackson for NPR
hide caption
toggle caption i
Malcolm Jackson for NPR
CUMBERLAND ISLAND, Ga.— Wild horses, feral hogs and deer roam free on this 18-mile barrier island, one of the largest and most ecologically diverse along the Atlantic coast. The landscape includes salt marshes, maritime forests, and an expansive stretch of pristine, untouched beach only accessible to the public by ferry.
Since 1972, the National Park Service has managed Cumberland Island National Seashore, including roughly 9,800 acres of wilderness designated by an act of Congress which stated that "the seashore shall be permanently preserved in its primitive state."
